title: Saber Interactive 的 Tim Willits 谈生成式 AI、研发迁出北美与拥抱知名 IP
content:
Saber Interactive's Tim Willits on generative AI, moving development out of North America, and embracing recognisable IP | GamesIndustry.biz

Saber Interactive has achieved a lot in the past few years, but the most noticeable recent news to come out of the the company was CEO Matthew Karch's
unfiltered response to accusations that a writer had been replaced with ChatGPT
. When we sit down at Gamescom for the second of two conversations with Saber Interactive's chief creative officer Tim Willits, it's the first thing we ask about.
"That's just Matt's sarcasm, that's all," he says. "But the important thing is that we've never replaced anybody with AI. That's crazy. And we don't use generative AI in Space Marine, and Hellraiser, and Stuntman, and everything.
"But we are experimenting with it, because we don't know where in the industry it's going to be effective, where people will like it, where it's useful. In
Rideshare Stimulator
, we are experimenting with it with the AI mode. Very clear that the other stuff was all written by humans. Even the side missions were all written by humans."
Rideshare Stimulator's Free Ride mode includes AI-generated passenger missions  |
Image credit:
Unigine/Saber Interactive
He believes that in the future, we will probably see a developer "come up with such a clever and brilliant use case for true modern AI integration,  everyone will be like, 'Oh, that's it', and everyone will understand that that's how it can be. But until that happens, it's like other technologies throughout history. When they first come out, people are like, 'What are we going to do with this technology? How's it going to work?' And then we all discover that it'll fit into everyday life."
Willits says that Saber doesn't use generative AI in its production pipelines for things like code, environments, or textures. But he does see the benefits of the technology. "One of the things that I always wished that I could do in my career is draw, because I always felt I would have been a better designer if I could actually draw… So for me, one of the things that helps me is if I can have a vision in my head and I need a way to get it out, it's something that I can definitely use."
"It will be interesting to see where it goes. And I bet at next year's Gamescom, I think we'll have some bigger games that actually focus on it. And I'm curious to see how it plays out for us, I'm curious to see how it works in our Rideshare game, and how people are going to like it. It's a great experiment."
Eggs and baskets
Saber Interactive
split from Embracer in 2024
, in a process that Willits describes as "very easy".  It remains a huge company, numbering 3,500 employees spread across 15 studios in places like Serbia, Armenia, Georgia, Spain, Portugal, Sweden, Argentina, and Australia. "Now that we've started a game in Australia, the sun no longer sets on Saber development," says Willits.
Saber will be releasing the first-person action horror survival game Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival in October  |
Image credit:
Saber Interactive
Notably, North America doesn't appear on that list. The firm has "no real development in North America any more," says Willits, although the company retains its headquarters in Florida and a publishing team based in the USA.
It's a sign of the times: as
ASGC's Amir Satvat put it
, "Head count moving from basically North America to basically anywhere else." Saber has embraced this. "We are not afraid of any territories. Some publishers are afraid to work in territories they don't understand, but we're like, let's go, let's find some people that are talented, let's give them what they need, and let's make awesomeness. You don't need to be in California to be a brilliant programmer or artist or animator."
Willits is the guy who's keeping it all ticking over. "My job is to just make sure the teams have what they need, make sure that they're focusing on what's key, make sure scope doesn't get out of hand," he says. And there's a lot to keep an eye on.
"People have heard me criticise old-fashioned modern publishers that put all their eggs in one basket: they have these siloed teams that focus on one project," says Willits. Saber, by contrast, has a lot of eggs, and a lot of baskets, along with the flexibility to move teams across projects as needed.
Jurassic Park: Survival takes place the day after the events of the 1993 movie  |
Image credit:
Saber Interactive
The company has its tentpole releases, like the upcoming games Stuntman: Hollywood, John Wick, Turok: Origins, and Jurassic Park: Survival. It pairs them with what Willits calls its "bread and butter stuff", like the remaster of the original Hitman trilogy, which follows remasters of Tomb Raider, Crysis, and Halo. "That's predictable, consistent work where you make money," he says.
"And then we have our smaller bets, like
Docked
and
Bus Bound
. Rideshare's like that. They're predictable, we know what we're going to spend, we can predict what we'll make. And then we have a culture that lets people work on all different games. So nobody feels that they're only on game A or game B, and we can pull resources from around the world to put the attention on a game when it's needed."
Docked, released earlier this year, is a realistic dock simulator  |
Image credit:
Saber Interactive
Willits says Saber is also exploring movie-style external development models. "We are talking to groups of people, like 18 to 20 super-talented developers in the US, that we can partner with. They bring the creativity and the genius and the vision, and we can bring the manpower. And instead of having 300 people sitting around in California waiting for the concept art to get done and just burning through that money, you can have a small group that focuses on the important things, and then we bring people in."
